title: Iterative Optimization Check
description: Predict the complexity tag for brute force, better, and optimal narration steps.

questions.prompt: For "find two numbers in an array that sum to a target," what is the complexity of the brute-force nested-loop approach?
questions.explanation: Checking every pair with nested loops examines roughly n^2 pairs — the classic brute-force complexity.

questions.prompt: Sorting the array first, then using two pointers moving inward, lands at which complexity for the two-sum problem?
questions.explanation: The two-pointer scan itself is O(n), but the initial sort costs O(n log n), which dominates the overall complexity.

questions.prompt: Using a hash map to record numbers seen so far and checking `target - number` in one pass reaches which complexity?
questions.explanation: A single pass with constant-time hash map lookups gives O(n) — the optimal approach for two-sum.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers often weight narrating the brute force → better → optimal journey, rather than just seeing the final optimal code?

options.text: Narration is required by law in technical interviews
It demonstrates the ability to reason about trade-offs and complexity incrementally, not just recall a memorized solution
Brute force is always the correct final answer
Narration replaces the need to write any code at all

questions.explanation: Talking through the improvement steps and their complexity shows genuine problem-solving, which can score higher than silently writing optimal code.

questions.prompt: What resource is typically traded for time when moving from an O(n^2) brute-force approach to an O(n) hash-map approach?

options.text: Space (extra memory for the hash map)
Nothing is traded — it's strictly better in every dimension

questions.explanation: The hash map approach uses extra memory to store seen values, trading space for the faster O(n) time complexity.

questions.prompt: For "check if a string has any repeated characters," what data structure typically gets you from a brute-force O(n^2) comparison to an optimal approach?

options.text: A set (or equivalent hash-based structure) to track seen characters
A sorted array with binary search

questions.explanation: Tracking seen characters in a set lets you detect a repeat in a single O(n) pass, replacing the pairwise O(n^2) comparison.
